issues.legal_issue: A cultivator whose holding in a permanently settled estate is not shown to have begun under the landholder may hold pre-existing occupancy rights that pass to successors, rather than acquiring those rights only under later legislation.
material_facts: The land lay within a permanently settled estate, and the cultivator had cultivated it during his lifetime.
There was no evidence that the cultivator or his predecessors had been inducted by the landholder, or of the terms or commencement of their occupation.
The cultivator and his descendants remained in uninterrupted possession until the relevant legislation came into force.
Annual written rent documents contained restrictive terms, but there was no reliable evidence that the landholder had evicted the family or that the documents reflected a new, precarious tenancy.
issues.conclusion: The cultivator held occupancy rights in the land; those rights devolved on his successors and were not first acquired under the later legislation.
issues.legal_principle: Where a ryot’s holding in a permanently settled estate is not shown to have commenced after the settlement, the presumption is that the landholder held the melvaram and the ryot held the kudivaram, with a right to remain in possession while regularly paying rent. The court relied on Venkata Narasimha Naidu v. Dandamudi Kotayya, Appa Rau v. Subbanna, Vencata Mahalakshmamma v. Ramajogi, Siva Subramanya v. Secretary of State for India, Secretary of State v. Vira Rayan, Cheekati Zamindar v. Banasooru Dhora, and Kumbham Lakshmanna v. Tanjirala Venkateswarlu. Section 6 of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, granted permanent occupancy rights to qualifying ryots in possession when it came into force, but did not establish that occupancy rights could not already exist.

rule.if: permanently_settled_estate and ryot_holding and (holding_commencement_unproved or holding_not_shown_to_begin_under_landholder) and uninterrupted_family_possession and not reliable_proof_of_terminable_tenancy

predicates.permanently_settled_estate: The land was situated in an estate subject to a permanent settlement.
predicates.ryot_holding: A cultivator held and cultivated the land as a ryot.
predicates.holding_commencement_unproved: The evidence did not establish when or on what terms the cultivator or predecessors began occupying the land.
predicates.holding_not_shown_to_begin_under_landhol: The evidence did not show that the cultivator or predecessors were inducted onto the land by the landholder.
predicates.uninterrupted_family_possession: The cultivator and successors remained in possession of the land without interruption.
predicates.reliable_proof_of_terminable_tenancy: Reliable evidence established that the cultivator’s occupation was under a tenancy liable to termination by the landholder.

issues.definition: When a ryot holds land in a permanently settled estate, the commencement of the holding is unproved or not shown to have begun under the landholder, the family remains in possession, and no reliable proof establishes a terminable tenancy, the ryot’s occupancy rights are treated as pre-existing and as devolving on successors.

issues.legal_issue: The presumption concerning a ryot’s rights in a permanently settled estate applies in a dispute among persons claiming through the ryot, as well as in a suit brought by the landholder against the ryot.
material_facts: The dispute was among family members claiming interests in land through the original cultivator, rather than a suit by the landholder against him.
The original cultivator’s occupation and the commencement and terms of the holding were not shown to have begun under the landholder.
issues.conclusion: The presumption based on the land-tenure system and local custom applies in a suit between persons claiming under the ryot.
issues.legal_principle: The presumption is rooted in the system of land tenure and the custom of the area, not merely in the procedural burden on a party asserting title; it therefore applies between persons claiming under the ryot as well as in an ejectment suit by the landholder. The court relied on the principles in Venkata Narasimha Naidu v. Dandamudi Kotayya and Vencata Mahalakshmamma v. Ramajogi, among the authorities reviewing ryot rights in permanently settled estates.

predicates.dispute_between_claimants_under_ryot: The proceeding is a dispute between people asserting rights through a cultivator, rather than a claim by the landholder against the cultivator.
predicates.ryot_holding: A cultivator held and cultivated the land as a ryot.
predicates.holding_commencement_unproved: The evidence did not establish when or on what terms the cultivator or predecessors began occupying the land.

issues.definition: If people dispute rights through a ryot whose holding’s commencement is unproved, the presumption about the ryot’s rights applies between those claimants.

issues.legal_issue: A court may not award past mesne profits for a period earlier than the period for which they were claimed.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed past mesne profits for a specified period before the suit.
The High Court awarded past mesne profits beginning earlier than the period claimed.
issues.conclusion: The award was modified so that past mesne profits were limited to the period claimed in the suit.
issues.legal_principle: A court cannot grant past mesne profits for a period that the plaintiff did not claim; the award must remain within the relief sought.

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking partition and separate possession of a share in property.
predicates.mesne_profits_claimed_for_limited_period: The plaintiff sought past mesne profits only for a specified period.
predicates.award_exceeds_claimed_period: The court awarded past mesne profits for a period earlier than the period the plaintiff claimed.

issues.definition: In a partition suit, if past mesne profits are claimed only for a specified period but the award extends earlier, the award is confined to the claimed period.
